definition: Eradicate means to destroy or wipe out completely.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word eradicate. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know eradicate should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: After the third infestation in two years, the landlord hired a crew with orders to eradicate the termites — every colony, every queen.
Curb sits far below eradicate — the numbers stop climbing, but the problem lives on where it is, nothing like the zero eradicate demands.
Contain goes further than curb — the outbreak is penned inside a boundary — but eradicate claims the most: nothing left to pen, anywhere.

To eliminate is to get rid of something, with no promise about completeness — a team eliminated from one tournament is back the next year. To eradicate is to wipe out completely: zero left, anywhere, ever. Elimination clears a space; eradication ends the line.

To exterminate is to kill off living things, usually pests, and the word stays close to actual killing. Eradicate reaches wider — you can eradicate a disease, an illegal practice, or a stubborn error, none of which die in the exterminator's sense — and it always promises zero.

Screwworm flies once cost American ranchers millions of animals a year.

Starting in the 1950s, technicians raised billions of the flies, sterilized the males with radiation, and dropped them from airplanes week after week; wild females that mated with them left no offspring.
Territory by territory the map went clean, and by 1966 the United States had eradicated the pest — not rare, gone.
Eradicate is the exact word for that campaign, because it means to destroy or wipe out completely — the goal is zero, not fewer.
The word's own anatomy says so: e- plus radix, to pull out by the root, the gardener's one guarantee that a weed will not return.
Reduce and control leave survivors; eradicate ends the line.
formal / campaign language
Eradicate is the word for campaigns against living, spreading things — diseases, pests, stubborn practices — and it promises zero.
Its unit-mates divide the labor: obliterate erases all trace of a thing, raze levels a structure to the ground, and pillage merely robs.
If survivors remain, you have reduced or contained, not eradicated.

In 1967 the World Health Organization set itself a goal no one had ever achieved against any disease: not to control smallpox, but to eradicate it.
Control was the old ambition — fewer outbreaks, fewer deaths, the virus pushed back but always present somewhere, waiting.
The new campaign hunted the virus case by case.
Teams traced every infection, vaccinated everyone around it, and drew a ring the disease could not cross.
The last natural case appeared in Somalia in 1977.
Searchers spent three more years knocking on doors before anyone dared say the work was finished.
In 1980 the declaration came: zero cases, on every continent, forever.
No disease of humans had ever before been driven to nothing.
